name: Sauvignon Blanc

lines.s10: Sauvignon Blanc is the bright, bone dry white of Sancerre and Marlborough: grapefruit, gooseberry and cut grass with mouthwatering acidity.
lines.s20: Sauvignon Blanc is the grape of Sancerre in the Loire and of Marlborough in New Zealand. It is dry and vivid, with grapefruit, gooseberry and fresh cut grass, and it is usually made without oak to keep that snap.
lines.s45: Sauvignon Blanc is at home in the upper Loire, in Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, and it found a second home in Marlborough, New Zealand. It smells of grapefruit, gooseberry and fresh cut grass, and it is dry, light and sharply refreshing. Most of it is fermented cold in steel, with no oak, to keep that freshness. The Loire tends to be quieter and flinty, while Marlborough is louder, with passion fruit on top. It is a natural with goat's cheese, oysters or anything with green herbs. Its name comes from sauvage, the French word for wild.
lines.sale: Sauvignon Blanc is the wake up call on the list: cold, dry and bright with grapefruit and cut grass. Start with it beside the goat's cheese or the shellfish, before anything richer comes to the table.

glass.lead: Grapefruit, gooseberry and passion fruit over fresh cut grass, on a light, bone dry frame with piercing acidity.

ladder.where: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, Marlborough, Styria, Chile's Casablanca Valley
Bordeaux and Margaret River, often blended with Sémillon
Napa Valley, inland Sonoma and California's warmer valleys

glass.structure: Bone dry as a rule. Acidity high, alcohol moderate, body light to medium; a little rounder where it is blended with Sémillon or raised in barrel.

old.where: The upper Loire, led by Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé; Bordeaux; Styria
old.glass: Tends to be restrained and taut: grapefruit, lime and green apple with cut grass and a smoky, struck flint edge, bone dry, with high acidity and moderate alcohol. In Bordeaux it is usually blended with Sémillon and rounder.
old.cellar: Usually fermented cool in steel and bottled young, with no new oak; some rest on their lees, and Pessac-Léognan often ferments in barrel.

new.where: Marlborough, Chile's Casablanca Valley, California, South Africa and the Adelaide Hills
new.glass: Typically louder and more pungent: passion fruit, guava and pink grapefruit over cut grass and green bell pepper, with high acidity. California is often softer and rounder, with melon and white peach.
new.cellar: Mostly fermented cold in steel and sold within the year, under the grape's own name; California's Fumé Blanc has often seen some oak.

contrast.why: Marlborough's bright sun, long days and cool nights build intense aroma and hold the acidity; the upper Loire, far inland on limestone and flint, gives quieter fruit. The Loire label names the village, the New World the grape.
contrast.blur: Marlborough's cooler, windier Awatere Valley makes leaner, greener wines, and a warm year gives Sancerre riper, rounder fruit; barrels appear on both sides.
contrast.call: Restraint, green apple and struck flint lean Loire; pungent passion fruit and guava over loud cut grass lean Marlborough.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius; a barrel fermented white Bordeaux a little warmer.
service.glass: A white wine glass: the smaller bowl keeps it cold and focuses the scent.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary: pour it cold and fresh from the bottle.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within two or three years; barrel fermented white Bordeaux and a few Sancerres keep longer.

with.dish: Goat's cheese, fresh or lightly aged
with.why: the Loire's own match: acidity meets the tang
the acidity works like a squeeze of lemon
acidity and green notes stand up to the sharp sauce
the wine's own grassy side welcomes them

labels.means: Upper Loire place names whose white wines are Sauvignon Blanc; the label names the place, not the grape.
A California name from the 1960s for dry Sauvignon Blanc, often aged in oak; a nod to Pouilly-Fumé.
White Bordeaux: Sauvignon Blanc usually blended with Sémillon, and in Pessac-Léognan often fermented in barrel.
The New Zealand region that made the pungent, passion fruit style known.

guest.a: Yes. White Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc from the upper Loire, and so is Pouilly-Fumé across the river. They tend to be quieter and flintier than a New Zealand one.

guest.q: What is the difference between Fumé Blanc and Sauvignon Blanc?
guest.a: It is the same grape. Fumé Blanc is a name California gave its dry Sauvignon Blanc in the 1960s, and a bottle that wears it has often seen some oak.

guest.q: I find New Zealand Sauvignon Blanc too grassy. What else is there?
guest.a: Try a Sancerre for something quieter and flinty, or a white Bordeaux, where Sémillon rounds it out.

compare.tell: Grüner Veltliner shows white pepper and lentil where Sauvignon Blanc shows cut grass and gooseberry, and it feels a little broader in the mouth.
Verdejo is grassy too, but it adds fennel and a faintly bitter finish; Sauvignon Blanc is sharper, with more grapefruit and gooseberry.
Albariño trades the grass for white peach, apricot and a salty finish; Sauvignon Blanc is greener and more pungent.

cards.front: Sauvignon Blanc: its home in the Loire, and the red grape it parented?
cards.back: Sancerre and Pouilly-Fumé, in the upper Loire. With Cabernet Franc it is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon, shown by DNA work published in 1997.

cards.front: Sauvignon Blanc blind: Loire or Marlborough, what tips it?
cards.back: Restraint, green apple and a smoky, struck flint note lean Loire. Pungent passion fruit and guava over loud cut grass lean Marlborough.

cards.front: What does Fumé Blanc mean on a California label?
cards.back: Sauvignon Blanc. The name was coined in California in the 1960s for a dry style, a nod to Pouilly-Fumé, and the wine has often seen some oak.

questions.q: A blind white is pale and bone dry, and pungent from the first sniff: passion fruit, guava and pink grapefruit over loud cut grass, with high acidity and no oak. Which origin fits it?
questions.exp: Pungent passion fruit and guava over cut grass at high acidity is the Marlborough signature. Sancerre tends to be quieter and flinty, and Pessac-Léognan and Napa are often rounder, with vanilla from barrels or ripe melon.

questions.q: A guest orders the warm goat's cheese and asks for the white that grows beside it in the upper Loire. Which bottle do you bring?
questions.exp: Sancerre is Sauvignon Blanc from the upper Loire, where goat's cheese is the local match. Vouvray is Chenin Blanc from the middle Loire, Muscadet comes from the Atlantic end, and Chablis is Burgundy.

questions.q: A dry white Bordeaux is poured: grapefruit and cut grass, but rounder and waxier than a Sancerre. Which grape is usually blended with the Sauvignon Blanc?
questions.exp: White Bordeaux usually blends Sauvignon Blanc with Sémillon, which adds body and a waxy texture. Chenin Blanc and Melon de Bourgogne belong to the Loire, not to Bordeaux.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it. The Codex's records on Sauvignon Blanc read true and nothing here departs from them; say opens on the Court's own respelling.
Gooseberry sits in the orchard fruit group for want of a nearer family among the nineteen.
The origin is left unstated: the Davis grape book calls it unknown, the Loire or the south west of France, so the entry says only where the grape is at home.
Fumé Blanc is dated to the 1960s and to California with no person named; the Davis grape book and the federal list of grape names both support the synonym.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open nzwine.com or bordeaux.com directly.

checked.verdict: Sound after three fixes. The facts, the four lines, the cards and the questions stand.
changed: worlds.contrast.why: the upper Loire is no longer called cooler than Marlborough. Sancerre is semi continental, far inland, with short hot summers; Marlborough is cool, sunny and maritime. The line now sets the sun, the long days and the cool nights of the one against the inland limestone and flint of the other.

worlds.contrast.blur: Martinborough is taken out, since no source read describes its Sauvignon Blanc as leaner and stonier. The Awatere Valley is said as the regional body says it, cooler and windier, and a warm year gives Sancerre riper, rounder fruit where the fragment promised passion fruit that no source confirmed.
glass.ladder, the warm rung: Sonoma narrowed to inland Sonoma, since its coast and the Russian River are cool.
open: No source address could be opened in this session, which reached search alone. The Davis news address was seen in a search listing; the others stand as the author gave them.
